approachQuestion.prompt:
Keep Samples at or Above the Threshold

Given an array `samples` and a threshold `cutoff`, return only the values greater than or equal to the threshold, preserving their original order.

Example 1: samples = [4, −2, 7, 1, 8], cutoff = 4 → [4, 7, 8].
Example 2: samples = [−3, −1], cutoff = 0 → [].
Example 3: samples = [5, 5], cutoff = 5 → [5, 5].
constraints: The input array may be overwritten.
The returned sequence is the output; its storage does not count as auxiliary space.

options.text: Scan from left to right. Write each retained value at the next output position, never beyond the current read position. Return the retained prefix.
options.feedback: The read/write boundary preserves every qualifying value in its original order. You only overwrite positions that have already been read.

options.text: Scan the input once and append each value that meets the threshold to a new output array.
options.feedback: This also preserves order and returns the required values. The new array is the output itself, whose storage the prompt excludes from auxiliary space, so this is an equally valid method.

options.text: Whenever you find a value below the threshold, remove it by shifting every later value one position to the left.
options.feedback: The result is correct and stable, but each removal shifts all later values. The same positions may be shifted repeatedly; the read/write boundary avoids those repeated shifts.

options.text: Sort the values in ascending order and return the suffix containing values greater than or equal to the threshold.
options.feedback: Sorting changes the order of the retained readings. For samples = [7, 2, 6] and cutoff = 6, the required result is [7, 6], not [6, 7].

feedback.reason: Choose a method that preserves the order of every value meeting the threshold. Both stable one-pass methods are correct; the method analyzed in the next question uses a read/write boundary.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the method “Read/Write Boundary,” choose one pair: time and auxiliary space. The input and the returned output are excluded from auxiliary space.
constraints: The input array may be overwritten.
The returned sequence is the output; its storage does not count as auxiliary space.

options.text: O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space when the result is written by stably overwriting the input.
O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space because every returned array always counts as auxiliary space.
O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space.

feedback.reason: Each input value is read once, and each retained value is written at most once. The read index and write boundary are the only helper variables. The result can be the stable prefix of the overwritten input, so no additional structure that grows with n is needed.
details: linear-constant: the tight pair for the selected in-place method.
linear-output: this incorrectly counts the output itself as auxiliary space; the prompt explicitly excludes it.
quadratic-constant: this describes repeated shifting after removals, not the read/write boundary method.
nlogn-linear: this describes unused sorting and copying, which also breaks stability.
Learning objective: Preserve the order of retained items and reason about the boundary between reading and writing.

methodReveal.title: Read/Write Boundary
methodReveal.description: Read values from left to right. When a value meets the threshold, write it at the next free position in the prefix. At the end, the prefix contains the result in its original order; the remaining suffix is not part of the result.
